canonical quantization is a procedure for [quantizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantization_(physics)) a [classical theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_theory), while attempting to preserve the formal structure, such as [symmetries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_(physics)), of the classical theory to the greatest extent possible.

definition: carpenter's rule problem is a [discrete geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_geometry) problem, which can be stated in the following manner: Can a [simple planar polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_polygon) be moved continuously to a position where all its vertices are in [convex position](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_position), so that the edge lengths and simplicity are preserved along the way? A closely related problem is to show that any non-self-crossing [polygonal chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygonal_chain) can be straightened, again by a continuous transformation that preserves edge distances and avoids crossings.

Cartan–Karlhede algorithm is a procedure for completely classifying and comparing [Riemannian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold)s.

Cartan–Kähler theorem is a major result on the [integrability conditions for differential systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrability_conditions_for_differential_systems), in the case of [analytic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_function)s, for [differential ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_ideal)s transl.

Cartesian coordinate system (, ) in a [plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(geometry)) is a [coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_system) that specifies each [point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_(geometry)) uniquely by a pair of [real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number)s called coordinates, which are the [signed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_and_negative_numbers) distances to the point from two fixed [perpendicular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular) [oriented line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriented_line)s, called [coordinate line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinate_line)s, coordinate axes or just axes (plural of axis) of the system.
Cartesian monoid is a [monoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoid), with additional structure of pairing and projection operators.
Cartier duality is an analogue of [Pontryagin duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_duality) for commutative [group scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_scheme)s.

Cartwright's theorem is a mathematical [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem) in [complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis), discovered by the British mathematician [Mary Cartwright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cartwright).

Car–Parrinello molecular dynamics (CPMD) refers to either a method used in molecular dynamics (also known as the Car–Parrinello method) or the [computational chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_chemistry) software package used to implement this method.

Casas-Alvero conjecture is an [open problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_problem) about [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial)s which have factors in common with their [derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative)s, proposed by [Eduardo Casas-Alvero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eduardo_Casas-Alvero) in 2001.

Casorati–Weierstrass theorem describes the behaviour of [holomorphic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_function)s near their [essential singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_singularity).

Castigliano's method, named after [Carlo Alberto Castigliano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlo_Alberto_Castigliano), is a method for determining the displacements of a [linear-elastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_elasticity) system based on the [partial derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_derivative)s of the [energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy).

Catalan's conjecture (or Mihăilescu's theorem) is a [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem) in [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory) that was [conjectured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjecture) by the mathematician [Eugène Charles Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugène_Charles_Catalan) in 1844 and [proven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_proof) in 2002 by [Preda Mihăilescu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preda_Mihăilescu) at [Paderborn University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paderborn_University).

concentration of measure (about a [median](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median)) is a principle that is applied in [measure theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure_theory), [probability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability) and [combinatorics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorics), and has consequences for other fields such as [Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space) theory.

Condensed mathematics is a theory developed by [Dustin Clausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dustin_Clausen) and [Peter Scholze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Scholze) which replaces a topological space by a certain sheaf of sets, in order to solve some technical problems of doing [homological algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homological_algebra) on [topological group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group)s.

conditional dependence is a relationship between two or more [events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Event_(probability_theory)) that are [dependent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dependence_(probability_theory)) when a third event occurs.

conditional event algebra (CEA) is an alternative to a standard, [Boolean algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra) of possible events (a set of possible events related to one another by the familiar operations and, or, and not) that contains not just ordinary events but also conditional events that have the form .

conditional expectation, conditional expected value, or conditional mean of a [random variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_variable) is its [expected value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value) evaluated with respect to the [conditional probability distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_probability_distribution).
conditional independence describes situations in which an observation is irrelevant or redundant when evaluating the certainty of a hypothesis.

conditional probability is a measure of the [probability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability) of an [event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Event_(probability_theory)) occurring, given that another event (by assumption, presumption, assertion, or evidence) is already known to have occurred.

conditional proof is a [proof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_proof) that takes the form of asserting a [conditional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Material_conditional), and proving that the [antecedent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antecedent_(logic)) of the conditional necessarily leads to the [consequent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequent).
conditional variance is the [variance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance) of a [random variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_variable) given the value(s) of one or more other variables.

conductance is a parameter of a [Markov chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain) that is closely tied to its [mixing time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_mixing_time), that is, how rapidly the chain converges to its [[Discrete-time Markov chain#Stationary distributions|stationary distribution]], should it exist.

confounding is a form of systematic error (or bias) that can distort estimates of causal effects in observational studies.

congruence (more properly, a congruence of curves) is the set of [integral curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_curve)s of a (nowhere vanishing) [vector field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_field) in a four-dimensional [Lorentzian manifold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentzian_manifold) which is interpreted physically as a model of [spacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacetime).
congruence is the set of [integral curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_curve)s defined by a nonvanishing [vector field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_field) defined on the manifold.
congruence coefficient is an index of the similarity between factors that have been derived in a [factor analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factor_analysis).

congruence lattice problem asks whether every algebraic [distributive lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributive_lattice) is [isomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphic) to the [congruence lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_lattice) of some other lattice.
congruence of squares is a [congruence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic) commonly used in [integer factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_factorization) algorithms.

congruence relation (or simply congruence) is an [equivalence relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation) on an [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) (such as a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)), [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics)), or [vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_space)) that is compatible with the structure in the sense that [algebraic operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_operation)s done with equivalent elements will yield equivalent elements.

congruent number is a positive [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) that is the [area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area) of a [right triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_triangle) with three [rational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number) sides.

[constructive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructive_proof) quantum field theory is the field devoted to showing that [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory) can be defined in terms of precise mathematical structures.

constructive set theory is an approach to [mathematical constructivism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructivism_(mathematics)) following the program of [axiomatic set theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiomatic_set_theory).

consumer-resource models (CRMs) are a class of [ecological model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecological_model)s in which a [community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_(ecology)) of consumer species compete for a common pool of resources.

method of (hypergraph) containers is a powerful tool that can help characterize the typical structure and/or answer extremal questions about families of discrete objects with a prescribed set of local constraints.

context model (or context modeling) defines how context data are structured and maintained (It plays a key role in supporting efficient context management).

Context-free language reachability is an [algorithmic problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithmic_problem) with applications in [static program analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Static_program_analysis).

Contextualization in [sociolinguistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociolinguistics) refers to the use of language (both spoken language and body language) to signal relevant aspects of an interaction or communicative situation.

continuity correction is an adjustment made when a [discrete object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_mathematics) is approximated using a [continuous object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function).

Continuous analytics is a [data science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_science) process that abandons [ETLs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extract,_transform,_load) and complex batch [data pipelines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_pipeline) in favor of [cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_computing)-native and [microservices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microservices) paradigms.

continuous linear operator or continuous linear mapping is a [continuous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function_(topology)) [linear transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_transformation) between [topological vector space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_vector_space)s.

Continuous optimization is a branch of [optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimization_(mathematics)) in [applied mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Applied_mathematics).

continuum hypothesis (abbreviated CH) is a hypothesis about the possible sizes of [infinite set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite_set)s.

Fourier transform on finite groups is a generalization of the [discrete Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_Fourier_transform) from [cyclic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclic_group) to arbitrary [finite group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_group)s.

Hilbert–Bernays paradox is a distinctive [paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradox) belonging to the family of the [paradoxes of reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_self–referential_paradoxes).

Hilbert–Bernays-Löb provability conditions, named after [David Hilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hilbert), [Paul Bernays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bernays), and [Martin Löb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Löb), are a set of requirements for formalized provability predicates in formal theories of arithmetic (Smith 2007:224).

Hilbert–Carleman determinant is an operator [determinant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant) for certain [integral operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_operator)s on [Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space)s, whose kernels are not necessarily [continuous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function).

Hilbert–Poincaré series (also known under the name [Hilbert series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_series)), named after [David Hilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hilbert) and [Henri Poincaré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Poincaré), is an adaptation of the notion of [dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension) to the context of [graded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graded_algebra) algebraic structures (where the dimension of the entire structure is often infinite).

Hilbert–Schmidt theorem, also known as the [eigenfunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenfunction) expansion theorem, is a fundamental result concerning [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_operator), [self-adjoint operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-adjoint_operator)s on [Hilbert space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_space)s.

Hilbert–Speiser theorem is a result on [cyclotomic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclotomic_field)s, characterising those with a [normal integral basis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_integral_basis).

metaplectic group is the [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) that describes how the basic symmetries of [classical mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_mechanics) act in [quantum mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanics).

method of Chester–Friedman–Ursell is a technique to find [asymptotic expansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymptotic_expansion)s for [contour integrals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contour_integration).

method of exhaustion () is a method of finding the [area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area) of a [shape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape) by [inscribing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inscribed_figure) inside it a [sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence) of [polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon)s (one at a time) whose [area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area)s [converge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limit_(mathematics)) to the area of the containing [shape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape).

method of fundamental solutions (MFS) is a technique for solving [partial differential equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_differential_equations) based on using the [fundamental solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_solution) as a basis function.
method of moments is a method of [estimation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estimation) of population [parameters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_parameter).

method of moments is a way of proving [convergence in distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_in_distribution) by proving convergence of a sequence of [moment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_(mathematics)) sequences.

method of steepest descent or saddle-point method is an extension of [Laplace's method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace's_method) for approximating an integral, where one deforms a contour integral in the [complex plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_plane) to pass near a [stationary point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stationary_point) ([saddle point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saddle_point)), in roughly the direction of steepest descent or stationary phase.

metric differential is a generalization of a [derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative) for a [Lipschitz continuous function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lipschitz_continuity) defined on a [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space) and taking values in an arbitrary [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space).

This repeats and the person who is first to lose both hands wins. ===Fifteen-Twenty=== Fifteen-Twenty is an old Chinese variant of morra with numerous variations of its own played in different parts of Asia. Two players face off in this game with both of their hands in front of them, face-to-face. Players take turns guessing the number of total fingers that are shown each round. Players can hold out either two fists (0), a fist and an open hand (5), or two open hands (10). As such, the total number of fingers that can be guessed is 0, 5, 10, 15, or 20. When a player makes a guess (a round), both players can change the number of fingers currently being held up. If the previous player made a wrong guess, the opponent can immediately start the new round and make a new guess without delay (sometimes catching the other player off guard before they are able to change their fingers). If a player guesses correctly, he immediately gets to guess again. Guessing correctly on the second try wins the game. If a player makes an impossible guess, (e.g. guessing 20 but only putting in a fist and a palm for 5 points) then that person gets a strike. Renormalization is a collection of techniques in [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory), [statistical field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_field_theory), and the theory of [self-similar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-similarity) geometric structures, that is used to treat [infinities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinity) arising in calculated quantities by altering values of these quantities to compensate for effects of their self-interactions Poincaré Seminar 2002, Progress in Mathematical Physics 30, Birkhäuser (2003) .

Reparenting is a form of [psychotherapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychotherapy) in which the therapist actively assumes the role of a new or surrogate parental figure for the client, in order to treat psychological disturbances caused by defective, even abusive, parenting.

Repeated measures design is a [research design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_design) that involves multiple measures of the same variable taken on the same or matched subjects either under different conditions or over two or more time periods.

repertory grid is an interviewing technique which uses [nonparametric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonparametric) [factor analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factor_analysis) to determine an [idiographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idiographic) measure of personality.

replicator equation is a type of [dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamical_system) used in [evolutionary game theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionary_game_theory) to model how the frequency of strategies in a population changes over time.
representation is a very general relationship that expresses similarities (or equivalences) between mathematical objects or [structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_structure).

representation theorem is a [theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem) that states that every abstract structure with certain properties is [isomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphic) to another (abstract or concrete) structure.

reprise ( , }} From the postmodern perspective, reprise is a fundamental [device](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_device) in the whole [history of art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_art).

Research Department () is a unit in the [IDF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Defense_Forces) [Directorate of Military Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aman_(IDF)) (Aman) that serves as the national assessor of [intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_(information_gathering)) in the [State of Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Israel).

Research in Number Theory is a [peer-reviewed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer-reviewed) [mathematics journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics_journal) covering [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory) and [arithmetic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_geometry).
Research Institute for Advanced Studies (RIAS) was among the several centers for research in the mathematical and physical sciences established throughout the United States after World War II.

definition: Reservoir sampling is a family of [randomized algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randomized_algorithm)s for choosing a [simple random sample](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_random_sample), without replacement, of items from a population of unknown size in a single pass over the items.
residence time is the average amount of time it takes for a [random process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_process) to reach a certain boundary value, usually a boundary far from the mean.

Residual income valuation (RIV), also called the residual income model or residual income method (RIM), is an approach to [equity valuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equity_valuation) that formally accounts for the [cost of equity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cost_of_equity) capital.

residuated Boolean algebra is a [residuated lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residuated_lattice) whose lattice structure is that of a [Boolean algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_(structure)).

residuated lattice is an [algebraic structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_structure) that is simultaneously a [lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_(order)) x ≤ y and a [monoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoid) x•y that admits operations x\z and z/y, loosely analogous to division or implication, when x•y is viewed as multiplication or [conjunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_conjunction), respectively.

residue of a function at a point of its domain is a [complex number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number) proportional to the [contour integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contour_integration) of a [meromorphic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meromorphic_function) along a path enclosing one of its [singularities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_singularity).

residue at infinity is a [residue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residue_(complex_analysis)) of a [holomorphic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_function) on an [annulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annulus_(mathematics)) having an infinite external radius.

residue theorem, sometimes called Cauchy's residue theorem, is a powerful tool to evaluate [line integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_integral)s of [analytic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_function)s over closed curves; it can often be used to compute real integrals and [infinite series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite_series) as well.

residue-class-wise affine [groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) are certain [permutation groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation_groups) [acting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action_(mathematics)) on , though only little work in this direction has been done so far.

resilience refers to the ability of a [dynamical system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamical_system) to recover from perturbations and return to its original [stable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stability_(mathematics)) [steady state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steady_state).

Resilience engineering is a subfield of [safety science research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_engineering) that focuses on understanding how [complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_system) [adaptive systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adaptive_systems) cope when encountering a surprise.

resolvent formalism is a technique for applying concepts from [complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis) to the study of the [spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_(functional_analysis)) of [operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_(mathematics))s on [Banach space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_space)s and more general spaces.

Resource selection functions (RSFs) are a class of functions that are used in [spatial ecology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spatial_ecology) to assess which [habitat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitat) characteristics are important to a specific population or species of animal, by assessing a probability of that animal using a certain resource proportional to the availability of that resource in the environment.

Response modeling methodology (RMM) is a general platform for statistical modeling of a linear/nonlinear relationship between a response variable ([dependent variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dependent_and_independent_variables)) and a linear predictor (a [linear combination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_combination) of predictors/effects/factors/[independent variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dependent_and_independent_variables)), often denoted the [linear predictor function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_predictor_function).

ring of restricted power series is the [subring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subring) of a [formal power series ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_power_series_ring) that consists of power series whose coefficients approach zero as degree goes to infinity.

Restricted stock, also known as restricted securities, is stock of a company that is not fully transferable (from the stock-issuing company to the person receiving the stock award) until certain conditions (restrictions) have been met.

restriction conjecture, also known as the Fourier restriction conjecture, is a conjecture about the behaviour of the [Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_transform) on curved hypersurfaces.

Results in Mathematics/Resultate der Mathematik is a [peer-reviewed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer-reviewed) [scientific journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_journal) that covers all aspects of pure and applied [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics) and is published by [Birkhäuser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkhäuser).

retraction is a [continuous mapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_mapping) from a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) into a [subspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subspace_topology) that preserves the position of all points in that subspace.

pole is a certain type of [singularity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singularity_(mathematics)) of a [complex-valued function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex-valued_function) of a [complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number) variable.
zero–one law is a result that states that an event must have probability 0 or 1 and no intermediate value.

ZetaGrid was at one time the largest [distributed computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_computing) project, designed to explore the non-trivial [root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_a_function)s of the [Riemann zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function), checking over one billion roots a day.

∞-groupoid is an abstract [homotopical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homotopical) model for [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space)s.

∞-topos (infinity-[topos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topos)) is, roughly, an [∞-category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/∞-category) such that its objects behave like [sheaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheaf_(mathematics)) of spaces with some choice of [Grothendieck topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_topology); in other words, it gives an intrinsic notion of sheaves without reference to an external space.

Sharp Satisfiability Problem (sometimes called Sharp-SAT, #SAT or model counting) is the problem of counting the number of [interpretations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpretation_(logic)) that [satisfy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satisfiability) a given [Boolean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_logic) [formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_(mathematical_logic)), introduced by Valiant in 1979.
